text: You've updated rows using a single WHERE condition. Now you'll narrow that further and update using values pulled from a second table through a join.

WHERE in an UPDATE supports the same operators you already use in SELECT. Combining Color equals Red with ListPrice greater than 1000 means only rows matching both conditions get the 10 percent discount -- everything else is left alone.

Sometimes the new value has to come from a different table. UPDATE ... FROM lets you join in a second table. Here, dbo dot LessonDemo is joined to Production dot Product on matching product names, and ListPrice is set to the real product's current price wherever ProductLine is R.

Notice UPDATE d names the alias, not the table name -- the real table only appears later in the FROM clause. This is the standard joined-update shape. A LessonDemo row with no match in Production dot Product is left untouched, exactly like an inner join would exclude it from a SELECT.

ON and WHERE do different jobs. ON decides which rows pair up in the join. An additional WHERE clause then filters those already-matched pairs further -- here, restricting the update to only pairs where the real product's price is over 500.
Next, you'll move from changing rows to removing them entirely with DELETE FROM.
